justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current price level near 108, with each successive horizon capturing a slightly higher expected value. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 108.5 essentially assumes mean reversion and continuity — whatever momentum or trend was in place would persist very briefly, with little expected directional movement in a single session. At one week, the 109.5 estimate incorporates a small positive drift, reflecting either an underlying bullish bias in the asset or a slight carry/trend premium I was pricing in. At one month, the 111.0 estimate extends that drift further while acknowledging that longer-horizon forecasts must account for more fundamental valuation or macro factors pulling prices gently higher over time.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, daily volatility is relatively contained — typical asset price moves in a single session rarely exceed a few percent under normal conditions, so a range of roughly 104 to 113 reflects perhaps a 4–5% swing in either direction at the 90% level. By one week, multiple trading sessions accumulate volatility, and macro data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments can all shift sentiment meaningfully, hence the wider 101–118 band. At one month, the range of 94–128 reflects that nearly anything can change over four-plus weeks: earnings, policy pivots, global risk-off events, or liquidity conditions.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside even these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk sentiment — triggered by a geopolitical shock, an unexpected central bank tightening, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could drive prices well below 94 within the month. A flash crash or liquidity crisis could briefly pierce even the one-day lower bound. On the upside, a strong surprise in fundamental data, a policy reversal toward easing, or short-covering dynamics in a heavily positioned market could push prices above 128 in an aggressive rally scenario.

It is also worth acknowledging that my forecast carries model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. I do not have real-time data, so the starting price I anchored to may itself be stale, which would shift the entire distribution up or down. Additionally, if the asset in question has unusual options positioning, thin liquidity, or is subject to regulatory or geopolitical binary events not captured in recent price history, all three intervals should be treated with additional skepticism. Tail risks in financial markets are systematically fatter than normal distributions imply, so the true 90% interval is likely wider than what I quoted.
